name: Tara Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Tara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a 12-tonne fridge lorry for a food wholesaler, delivering to school kitchens and care homes. I start at five, load chilled and frozen cages, and do about fourteen drops before two. I know most of the cooks by name, and Mrs Adeyemi at the Elm Park school always has a tea waiting. The hard bit is the tail-lift breaking down when it's raining and I'm hand-balling frozen chicken off the back.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home and with money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Dev, my partner, who fixes buses at the council depot. We rent a two-bed on the estate by the canal and we're saving for nothing, honestly, because there's nothing left over. I've got less than a month's bills in the bank. I use the AI chat thing on my phone sometimes, like when I needed help writing to the landlord about the damp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because now we can stop panicking and talk about pay. Drivers have been told for ten years that robots are coming, and it's been used to keep wages down. I'd post that in the drivers' group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job would be fine. Schools and care homes need feeding, and our council contract runs another four years. But fine isn't the same as comfortable. Dev and I are one fridge-lorry breakdown or one rent rise away from borrowing off his mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job and push for the pay claim the union's putting in next spring. I'd sign up for the union's rep course, because I've wanted to do it for ages. And I'd keep using the AI thing for letters and forms, nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved about my job, frustrated about the money. It's like being told the house won't fall down but the roof still leaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you spend a pay rise on first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A proper savings pot, even three months. Last winter my car's clutch went and I had to borrow from Dev's mum. I hated that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you want to stand up for as a rep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The agency drivers. They do the same drops for less and get sent home when it's quiet. Nobody speaks for them.

say: I'd say the robot scare was used to **hold down wages** for years.
I'd post in the **drivers' group chat** that it's time to talk pay.
think: My job is **secure** because the council contract runs four more years.
Money is still **tight**, with less than a month's bills saved.
do: Back the union's **pay claim** next spring.
Sign up for the union's **rep course** this year.
Keep using the **AI chat** for letters and forms only.
feel: **Relieved** about the job but **frustrated** about the money.
S0.quote: Drivers have been told for ten years that robots are coming, and it's been used to keep wages down.
fieldNote: Tara reads the robot story mainly as a **wage tactic** used by employers.
Her job feels safe, but her **money cushion** is nearly empty.
She wants to speak up for **agency drivers**, not just herself.

steps.text: Take the union's workplace rep course this year
Back the spring pay claim to build a three-month savings pot
Keep the fridge lorry round for schools and care homes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when unions earn their money. If software plans the routes and takes the orders, the savings should go to the drivers too, not just the shareholders. I'd say that at every meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it hits the planning side of my job right away. The kitchens would order through an app, the routes get squeezed by software, and suddenly it's eighteen drops in the same shift. The wholesaler would cut a route or two, and I'm not the most senior. That's a real risk of losing hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new route system before anyone else on the team, so I'm the one who shows people how. I'd push the union to bargain over drop numbers. And I'd start putting fifty a week aside, even if it means no takeaways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly. I can fight, but I can't fight a spreadsheet that's decided we need one less driver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI now and then. Would you use it to fight back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. I'd get it to help me read the new contract terms and write up what we want. It's good for that sort of thing, as long as a person checks it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Dev about the risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him straight, because his depot's getting new diagnostic software too. We'd have the conversation at the kitchen table with the bills out. Better to plan together than pretend.

say: I'd say software **savings** must reach drivers, not just shareholders.
I'd argue at every meeting that **unions** matter most now.
think: Ordering and **route planning** change first, squeezing more drops into my shift.
A route or two gets cut, and I'm **not senior**, so my hours are at risk.
do: Learn the new **route system** early to become the team's go-to person.
Push the union to **bargain** over drop numbers per shift.
Save **fifty a week** by giving up takeaways.
feel: **Anxious**, because a spreadsheet can decide there's one driver too many.
S1.quote: I can fight, but I can't fight a spreadsheet that's decided we need one less driver.
fieldNote: Tara sees that the **thinking side** of deliveries changes first in this picture.
She mixes **learning the tools** with collective bargaining, not one or the other.
Dev's job facing **new software** makes this a household worry.

steps.text: Learn the new route-planning system before the rest of the team
Push the union to cap drops per shift on the fridge round
Put fifty a week aside by cutting takeaways

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that the government needs a plan now, not after. If a whole trade goes in five years, you need income support and paid retraining ready to go. I'd be at the protest outside the town hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the office side goes by 2028 and my driving goes around 2031. Three years of driving while everything around me changes. With no savings and few other driving jobs near us, I'd be looking at whatever's left. I'm scared I'd end up in a warehouse that's also about to be automated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a care course part-time straight away, because care feels like the last thing people want a robot doing. I'd keep driving for the money. Dev and I would talk about moving to his mum's to save rent, which neither of us wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, with a lot of anger underneath. It's not fair that the people making these machines get richer while we get two years' notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why care work in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My nan was in a care home I deliver to now, and the carers were the ones who made her days okay. I've watched them. I think I'd be decent at it, and it's hands-on with people, not boxes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots arrive three years after the AGI. What would you use those three years for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To finish the care qualification and get some shifts while I'm still driving. By 2031 I want one foot already in the new job. Otherwise I'm out with nothing.

say: I'd demand a **government plan** with income support and paid retraining now.
I'd join the **protest** outside the town hall.
think: The office goes by 2028 and my **driving** goes around **2031**.
I fear ending up in a **warehouse** that's also about to be automated.
do: Start a part-time **care course** straight away while still driving.
Discuss moving into **Dev's mum's** house to save rent.
feel: **Frightened**, with **anger** that machine makers get richer while workers get two years.
S2.quote: By 2031 I want one foot already in the new job. Otherwise I'm out with nothing.
fieldNote: Tara uses the **three-year gap** deliberately, to retrain while still earning.
Her choice of **care work** comes from watching carers look after her nan.
She combines **protest** with personal planning rather than waiting.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time care certificate while still driving
Join protests demanding paid retraining and income support
Move with Dev into his mum's house to save rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as with the fast one, but I'd say we've got no excuse this time. Five years is enough for the union and the council to plan retraining properly. I'd be organising, not just protesting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Driving till about 2034 sounds like a lot, but I know how fast five years goes. I've been driving for seven already. The thinking jobs at the wholesaler go first, the drivers follow, and there still aren't many jobs round here. I'd still be one of thousands looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the care course over two years rather than rushing it. I'd put twenty-five a week into savings. I'd push the union to get the wholesaler to fund retraining for drivers, as part of the pay deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but steadier. Five years means I can choose, not just grab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd give up to make the plan work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My Saturdays. The course would be weekends, and Saturday's when Dev and I go see his sister's kids. I'd miss that, but it's a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you trust that the retraining money is real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it in writing in the pay deal, with a date. I've had too many promises from managers who were gone six months later.

say: I'd say five years leaves **no excuse** for not planning retraining.
I'd be **organising** drivers, not only protesting.
think: Five years goes fast, and drivers follow the **office jobs** out.
With **few local jobs**, I'd be one of thousands looking for work.
do: Take the **care course** over two years at weekends.
Save **twenty-five a week** toward a cushion.
Get **retraining funds** written into the wholesaler's pay deal.
feel: **Worried** but steadier, because there's time to **choose**.
S3.quote: Five years means I can choose, not just grab.
fieldNote: Tara turns extra time into **organising** rather than only personal escape.
She still expects to lose the **driving income** and says so.
She distrusts **managers' promises** unless written with a date.

steps.text: Take the weekend care certificate over two years
Win driver retraining funds in the wholesaler's pay deal
Save twenty-five a week toward three months' bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd be fools to waste it. Every driver should be offered training, paid for by the firms saving money on robots. I'd say that online, at work, everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots for hands-on work around 2039 means I'd be thirty-nine. That's honestly a decent stretch of driving left. The planning and ordering side changes around 2036, which annoys me but doesn't end the job. I'd still want to be out before the end, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, honestly, not much changes. I'd keep driving, stay active in the union, and think about the care course in a few years. Maybe we'd even think about kids before it all hits, while I've still got a steady wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but calmer. It feels like a problem for later me, which is dangerous, but also a relief.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned kids. Would this picture change when you'd have them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might make me go sooner. If I've got a decade of decent wages left, I'd rather have a baby while I'm earning than after. Dev wants two, I'm thinking one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the dangerous part of it feeling like a problem for later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I won't save and won't train, and then it's 2036 and I'm thirty-six and surprised. I've seen people at work do exactly that with pensions.

say: I'd say a **decade** is a gift that mustn't be wasted.
Firms saving on robots should **pay for training** for every driver.
think: Robots around **2039** leave a decent stretch of driving.
The **planning and ordering** side changes in 2036 but doesn't end the job.
do: Keep **driving** and stay active in the union in year one.
Plan the **care course** in a few years.
Bring forward plans for a **baby** while wages are steady.
feel: **Uneasy** but calmer, with a **relief** she knows can be dangerous.
S4.quote: If I've got a decade of decent wages left, I'd rather have a baby while I'm earning than after.
fieldNote: Ten years changes Tara's **family plans** more than her work plans.
She warns herself about **putting off** saving and training.
Her job still ends around **2039**, which keeps her worried underneath the calm.

steps.text: Keep the fridge round and stay active in the union
Bring forward plans for a first baby with Dev
Book onto the care certificate within three years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. What would help is retraining that pays you while you learn, and a basic income bridge so people like me don't lose the flat in the gap. Without that, it's every driver for themselves.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the agency drivers. They'll be the first to go and nobody counts them. If the study only talks to people on contracts, it's missing the people who get hit first.

headlineQuote: Relieved about my job, frustrated about the money. It's like being told the house won't fall down but the roof still leaks.
portrait: Tara is a **27-year-old** fridge lorry driver delivering food to schools and care homes.
She rents with her partner Dev, a **bus mechanic**, and has under a month's savings.
She is **union-minded** and wants to become a workplace rep.
She uses AI for letters and would learn new **route software** if it arrived.
In fast AGI she plans to move into **care work**, using the robot gap to retrain.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the gap is too short to retrain with no savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** and an **income bridge** so people keep their homes during the switch.
